description: Remediation playbook — structured steps for each detection rule. Readable by humans and machines.

autoplay_media.title: A video or a sound starts playing by itself
autoplay_media.risk: The autoplay attribute starts the video or sound as soon as the page opens. The sound covers the voice of the screen reader (software that reads the page aloud) that blind people listen to, and it surprises or distracts everyone else.

steps.action: Locate the vulnerable code pattern in the file
Remove the autoplay attribute and add controls, so that visitors start playback when they want.
Run the audit again to verify the finding is resolved

autoplay_media.benefit: Visitors choose when the media plays, and screen readers stay audible.

button_no_aria.title: A button that shows only an icon has no name
button_no_aria.risk: This <button> shows only an icon or an image, with no text and no aria-label. Blind people using a screen reader (software that reads the page aloud) hear only "button", without knowing what it does.

steps.action: Locate the vulnerable code pattern in the file
Add an aria-label that says what the button does, for example aria-label="Close", and alt="" on the image inside.
Run the audit again to verify the finding is resolved

button_no_aria.benefit: Screen reader users know what each button does.

catch_all_exception.title: An error handler catches everything, even a request to stop the program
catch_all_exception.risk: A bare except: catches every error, including the request to stop the program (Ctrl+C, SystemExit). Real failures, security errors among them, are then hidden, and the program goes on in a broken state.

steps.action: Locate the vulnerable code pattern in the file
Name the errors you expect, for example except (ValueError, OSError) as e:, write them to the logs, and let the others through.
Run the audit again to verify the finding is resolved

catch_all_exception.benefit: Unexpected failures stay visible and can be fixed.

catch_all_exception_csharp.title: An error handler catches every kind of error with catch (Exception)
catch_all_exception_csharp.risk: A catch (Exception ex) handles every error the same way, the expected ones and the bugs alike. Real failures are then hidden or wrongly reported, and the program goes on in a broken state.

steps.action: Locate the vulnerable code pattern in the file
Catch only the errors you expect, for example catch (IOException ex), write them to the logs with _logger.LogError(ex, "..."), and let the others through.
Run the audit again to verify the finding is resolved

catch_all_exception_csharp.benefit: Unexpected failures stay visible and can be fixed.

catch_all_exception_java.title: A catch block catches every kind of error at once
catch_all_exception_java.risk: The block catch (Exception e) catches every error, including programming mistakes such as a missing value. These errors are handled like expected ones and stay hidden, so bugs reach your users without anyone noticing.

steps.action: Locate the vulnerable code pattern in the file

Replace the generic catch: 1) catch only the errors you expect in this place, for example catch (IOException e) or catch (IOException | SQLException e); 2) let the other errors go up to the calling code.
Run the audit again to verify the finding is resolved

catch_all_exception_java.benefit: Programming mistakes show up instead of being silently hidden.

catch_all_exception_php.title: A catch block catches every exception without distinction
catch_all_exception_php.risk: catch (Exception $e) catches every exception, whatever its cause. Real failures, security errors among them, are then handled like an expected case or simply hidden, and the program goes on in a broken state.

steps.action: Locate the vulnerable code pattern in the file
Name the exceptions you expect, for example catch (InvalidArgumentException $e), write them to the logs, and let the others through.
Run the audit again to verify the finding is resolved

catch_all_exception_php.benefit: Unexpected failures stay visible and can be fixed.

client_side_auth.title: Access rights are read from the browser's local storage
client_side_auth.risk: The code decides who is an administrator from a value in localStorage (data kept by the browser), such as role or isAdmin. Any user can change that value in the browser tools and unlock admin features.

steps.action: Locate the vulnerable code pattern in the file
Check rights on the server for every request, and use the browser value only to choose what to display.
Run the audit again to verify the finding is resolved

client_side_auth.benefit: Changing a value in the browser no longer gives admin rights.

command_injection_csharp.title: Process.Start() launches a program, possibly with user data
command_injection_csharp.risk: Process.Start() launches a program on the machine with its arguments written as one line of text. If part of that text comes from a user, they can add options or, through cmd /c, their own commands, and take control of the server.

steps.action: Locate the vulnerable code pattern in the file

Launch the program directly, without cmd or a shell: 1) create a ProcessStartInfo with the program name; 2) add each argument with psi.ArgumentList.Add(value); 3) accept from the user only the values you expect.
Run the audit again to verify the finding is resolved

command_injection_csharp.benefit: A user value stays a single argument and can no longer start other commands.

command_injection_java.title: A system command is started with Runtime.exec()
command_injection_java.risk: Runtime.getRuntime().exec() runs a program on the server, often from a text built by joining pieces. If one piece comes from a visitor, they can add their own commands and take control of the server.

steps.action: Locate the vulnerable code pattern in the file

Replace the call: 1) pass the program and each argument separately to new ProcessBuilder("ping", "-c", "1", host), never as one joined string; 2) accept only expected values for each argument, for example a host name made of letters, digits, dots and dashes.
Run the audit again to verify the finding is resolved

command_injection_java.benefit: Visitor data can no longer add commands on your server.

command_injection_php.title: A system command is run with shell_exec, system or passthru
command_injection_php.risk: shell_exec(), system(), passthru(), popen(), proc_open() and backticks (`…`) hand a line of text to the shell (the program that runs system commands). If part of it comes from a user, a character such as ; lets them add their own command and take control of the server.

steps.action: Locate the vulnerable code pattern in the file

Pass every variable part through escapeshellarg() before building the command, for example shell_exec('ls ' . escapeshellarg($dir)), or, better, run the program with proc_open() and an array of arguments, which skips the shell.
Run the audit again to verify the finding is resolved

command_injection_php.benefit: No user data can turn into a command on your server.

console_log_residual.title: A console.log call is left in the code
console_log_residual.risk: Debug messages written with console.log stay in the version that runs for real. They appear in the browser console or the server logs, where others can read them, and may show data or how your application works.

steps.action: Locate the vulnerable code pattern in the file
Remove the call, or replace it with your logging library (logger.debug()), whose level you can turn off in production.
Run the audit again to verify the finding is resolved

console_log_residual.benefit: Debug messages no longer reach the people who use your application.

console_write_csharp.title: Messages are written to the console with Console.WriteLine
console_write_csharp.risk: The code prints messages with Console.Write or Console.WriteLine instead of the logger of the application. These messages have no level (debug, error), are neither kept nor filtered, and can show internal data in production.

steps.action: Locate the vulnerable code pattern in the file
Write the message through ILogger with the right level: _logger.LogDebug("Processing {Data}", data) for details, _logger.LogError(...) for failures.
Run the audit again to verify the finding is resolved

console_write_csharp.benefit: Your messages reach the logs with a level, and can be filtered or turned off.

cors_permissive_csharp.title: Any website can call your API from a visitor's browser
cors_permissive_csharp.risk: AllowAnyOrigin() or WithOrigins("*") sets the CORS policy (the browser rule that says which other sites may read your responses) to accept every site. A malicious page opened by your users can then read your API answers.

steps.action: Locate the vulnerable code pattern in the file
List only the sites you trust: policy.WithOrigins("https://app.example.com").
Run the audit again to verify the finding is resolved

cors_permissive_csharp.benefit: Only your own sites can read your API answers in the browser.

csv_injection.title: A CSV export can carry formulas that run in a spreadsheet
csv_injection.risk: This file writes a CSV without checking the values. A value that starts with =, +, - or @ becomes a formula when the file is opened in Excel or LibreOffice. Such a formula can send data elsewhere or run a command on the reader's computer.

steps.action: Locate the vulnerable code pattern in the file
Add a single quote in front of each value that starts with =, +, - or @ before writing it ("'" + value), for example in a small function called on every cell.
Run the audit again to verify the finding is resolved

csv_injection.benefit: Exported files open as plain data, with no formula run.

dangerous_eval.title: Dangerous Eval/Exec
dangerous_eval.risk: eval() or exec() with user data allows arbitrary code execution.

steps.action: Locate the vulnerable code pattern in the file
Never use eval/exec with external data.
Run the audit again to verify the finding is resolved
Locate the vulnerable code pattern in the file
Add database configuration in audit.config.json.
Run the audit again to verify the finding is resolved
Locate the vulnerable code pattern in the file
Check connection settings and credentials.
Run the audit again to verify the finding is resolved

db_logic_controller_csharp.title: A web controller talks to the database directly
db_logic_controller_csharp.risk: A controller (the class that answers web requests) opens connections or runs SQL itself. Database code spreads across the site, is hard to test, and every SQL change touches request-handling code.

steps.action: Locate the vulnerable code pattern in the file
Move the database code into a service class: 1) create the class (UserService) with the SqlConnection or DbContext; 2) pass it to the controller through its constructor and call _service.GetAll().
Run the audit again to verify the finding is resolved

db_logic_controller_csharp.benefit: Database access lives in one place and controllers stay simple to test.

db_logic_controller_java.title: A web controller talks to the database directly
db_logic_controller_java.risk: A class that answers web requests (@RestController, @GetMapping…) also runs SQL with Statement, PreparedStatement or JdbcTemplate. Web handling and data access are then mixed, so the code is hard to test and the same query gets copied in several places.

steps.action: Locate the vulnerable code pattern in the file

Move the database code out of the controller: 1) put the queries in a @Repository class and the business rules in a @Service class; 2) inject that service into the controller and call it, for example return orderService.findAll();.
Run the audit again to verify the finding is resolved

db_logic_controller_java.benefit: Each class has one job, so it is easier to test and change.

db_logic_controller_php.title: A controller sends its own queries to the database
db_logic_controller_php.risk: A file with a controller or routes (the code that answers web requests) also runs SQL queries, through DB::select(), DB::raw(), ->query() or mysqli_query(). The same query ends up copied in several places, and the code is harder to test and to change.

steps.action: Locate the vulnerable code pattern in the file
Move the queries into a separate class, for example a UserRepository with a getAll() method, and call that class from the controller.
Run the audit again to verify the finding is resolved

db_logic_controller_php.benefit: Each query lives in one place, where you can test and change it.

steps.action: Locate the vulnerable code pattern in the file
Check psql installation and permissions.
Run the audit again to verify the finding is resolved
Locate the vulnerable code pattern in the file
Install the required tool.
Run the audit again to verify the finding is resolved

debug_mode.title: Debug mode is turned on in the code
debug_mode.risk: With debug=True, an error shows the visitor details meant for developers: the code involved, the values of variables, the paths of files. An attacker learns how the application is built and where to attack.

steps.action: Locate the vulnerable code pattern in the file
Turn debug mode off in production: read it from an environment variable (debug = os.environ.get("DEBUG") == "true") so that it is only on for local development.
Run the audit again to verify the finding is resolved

debug_mode.benefit: Errors no longer show visitors how your application is built.

default_credentials.title: A default password (admin, root, changeme…) is written in the code
default_credentials.risk: This password is one of the first that attackers try, such as admin, root or 123456. If it stays in production, anyone can log in with it, often with full rights.

steps.action: Locate the vulnerable code pattern in the file
Remove the default password: 1) read the first password from an environment variable (os.environ["ADMIN_PASSWORD"]); 2) make the user choose a new one at the first login.
Run the audit again to verify the finding is resolved

default_credentials.benefit: No one can log in with a password everybody knows.

deprecated_api.title: The code calls a Python function that is outdated or removed
deprecated_api.risk: This function is deprecated (marked for removal), such as os.popen, tempfile.mktemp, distutils or optparse. Some already fail on recent Python versions, and tempfile.mktemp lets another program take the file name first.

steps.action: Locate the vulnerable code pattern in the file
Replace it with the current function: subprocess.run() instead of os.popen(), tempfile.mkstemp() instead of tempfile.mktemp(), argparse instead of optparse, setuptools instead of distutils.
Run the audit again to verify the finding is resolved

deprecated_api.benefit: The code keeps working on new Python versions.

deprecated_api_csharp.title: Outdated .NET class (WebClient, BinaryFormatter, JavaScriptSerializer…)
deprecated_api_csharp.risk: Microsoft marks these classes as obsolete: they get no improvements, and some, like BinaryFormatter, MD5 and SHA1, are unsafe. Recent .NET versions remove or block them, which can break your build.

steps.action: Locate the vulnerable code pattern in the file
Replace each class with its current version: HttpClient for WebClient, System.Text.Json for JavaScriptSerializer and BinaryFormatter, SHA256.Create() for SHA1Managed and MD5CryptoServiceProvider.
Run the audit again to verify the finding is resolved

deprecated_api_csharp.benefit: Your code keeps working on new .NET versions and avoids known weaknesses.

deprecated_api_java.title: Code uses Java methods marked as outdated
deprecated_api_java.risk: Methods such as Thread.stop(), suspend(), resume(), finalize() or new Date(year, month, day) are marked as outdated in Java. Some cause bugs that are hard to find, such as locked or corrupted data, and new Java versions may remove them. A @SuppressWarnings("deprecation") annotation also hides the compiler's warnings about them.

steps.action: Locate the vulnerable code pattern in the file

Remove the outdated calls: 1) replace stop(), suspend() and resume() with Thread.interrupt(), finalize() with try-with-resources, and new Date(...) with LocalDate.of(year, month, day); 2) delete the @SuppressWarnings("deprecation") annotation so the compiler warns you again.
Run the audit again to verify the finding is resolved

deprecated_api_java.benefit: The code keeps working on new Java versions and avoids known bugs.

deprecated_api_javascript.title: The code uses an outdated JavaScript feature
deprecated_api_javascript.risk: The code uses document.write(), escape(), unescape(), arguments.callee or sets __proto__. These features slow the page or fail in strict mode, and browsers may drop them.

steps.action: Locate the vulnerable code pattern in the file
Replace each outdated call with its modern form: element.textContent or append() for document.write(), encodeURIComponent() for escape(), and Object.setPrototypeOf() for __proto__.
Run the audit again to verify the finding is resolved

deprecated_api_javascript.benefit: Your code keeps working in current and future browsers.

deprecated_api_php.title: A PHP function removed from recent versions is still used
deprecated_api_php.risk: mysql_*(), ereg(), split(), each(), create_function(), mcrypt_*() and session_register() no longer exist in PHP 7 or 8. On an up-to-date server, the page stops with a fatal error, and some of these functions also have known security flaws. A call to trigger_error() with E_USER_DEPRECATED is reported too: it marks code that its authors plan to remove.

steps.action: Locate the vulnerable code pattern in the file

Replace each call with its current equivalent: 1) mysql_*() with PDO or mysqli; 2) ereg() and split() with preg_match() and preg_split(); 3) each() with foreach; 4) create_function() with function () { … }; 5) mcrypt_*() with openssl_encrypt() or sodium_crypto_secretbox(); 6) session_register() with $_SESSION['name'] = $value.
Run the audit again to verify the finding is resolved

deprecated_api_php.benefit: Your code runs on current PHP versions, which receive security fixes.

destructive_without_backup.title: The code deletes a whole table or all its rows
destructive_without_backup.risk: The code runs DROP, TRUNCATE or a DELETE without WHERE directly against the database. One wrong run, on the wrong database for example, erases the data for good, with no way to undo it.

steps.action: Locate the vulnerable code pattern in the file

Make each deletion deliberate: 1) change the structure of tables through a migration tool (Alembic, Django migrations) that can undo it; 2) add a WHERE clause to each DELETE; 3) take a backup before any mass deletion.
Run the audit again to verify the finding is resolved

destructive_without_backup.benefit: A mistake no longer destroys data you cannot get back.

django_csrf_exempt.title: A Django view turns off the check against requests from other websites
django_csrf_exempt.risk: @csrf_exempt removes from this view the CSRF check of Django (the proof that a request comes from your own pages). A page on another site can then make a logged-in visitor's browser send it, for example to change their password.

steps.action: Locate the vulnerable code pattern in the file
Remove @csrf_exempt and let Django check the request. For an API used without cookies, authenticate each request with a token sent in a header.
Run the audit again to verify the finding is resolved

django_csrf_exempt.benefit: Another website can no longer act in the name of your logged-in visitors.

django_debug_enabled.title: Django in debug mode: an error shows the code and settings
django_debug_enabled.risk: With DEBUG = True, every error page shows visitors the code involved, the SQL queries and most settings. An attacker learns how the application is built, and sometimes reads passwords in the settings.

steps.action: Locate the vulnerable code pattern in the file
Turn debug mode off in production: read it from an environment variable (DEBUG = os.environ.get("DJANGO_DEBUG") == "True") so that it is only on for local development.
Run the audit again to verify the finding is resolved

django_debug_enabled.benefit: Error pages no longer reveal your code and settings.

django_secret_key_weak.title: The secret key of Django is written in the code
django_secret_key_weak.risk: Django signs sessions, password reset links and form tokens with SECRET_KEY. Anyone who reads this key in the code can forge them, for example to log in as another user.

steps.action: Locate the vulnerable code pattern in the file

Remove the key from the code: 1) read it from an environment variable (SECRET_KEY = os.environ["DJANGO_SECRET_KEY"]); 2) generate a new one with get_random_secret_key(), since the old one stays in the history.
Run the audit again to verify the finding is resolved

django_secret_key_weak.benefit: Reading your code no longer lets anyone forge sessions or links.

dockerfile_copy_all.title: The Dockerfile copies the whole project into the image, secrets included
dockerfile_copy_all.risk: The line COPY . . copies the whole project folder into the Docker image, including secret files such as .env or keys. Anyone who gets the image can read them.

steps.action: Locate the vulnerable code pattern in the file

Limit what goes into the image: 1) next to the Dockerfile, create a .dockerignore file that lists .env, .git and your key files; 2) replace COPY . . with a copy of only the folders you need, for example COPY src/ ./src/.
Run the audit again to verify the finding is resolved

dockerfile_copy_all.benefit: Your secrets do not end up in the images you publish.

dockerfile_root_user.title: Your application runs as administrator in its container
dockerfile_root_user.risk: Without a USER line, the container runs your application with administrator rights (root). If it is hacked, the attacker gets these rights and can change anything in the container.

steps.action: Locate the vulnerable code pattern in the file
Add at the end of the Dockerfile, after installing the dependencies, a user without special rights: RUN adduser --disabled-password appuser then USER appuser.
Run the audit again to verify the finding is resolved

dockerfile_root_user.benefit: A flaw in your application does not give administrator rights.

dockerfile_unpinned_base.title: The Dockerfile's base image has no fixed version
dockerfile_unpinned_base.risk: The FROM line always takes the latest version of the base image. Your application can then change or break without you changing anything, or receive a booby-trapped version.

steps.action: Locate the vulnerable code pattern in the file
Give a precise version in the FROM line, for example FROM node:20-alpine instead of FROM node.
Run the audit again to verify the finding is resolved

dockerfile_unpinned_base.benefit: Every build of the image gives the same result, with a version you chose.

dom_manipulation_loop.title: Elements are added to the page one at a time
dom_manipulation_loop.risk: Inside a loop, the code inserts each element into the page with appendChild(), insertBefore() or innerHTML +=. Each insertion can make the browser recompute the page, which slows it down with long lists.

steps.action: Locate the vulnerable code pattern in the file
Insert the elements in one go: 1) create a container with document.createDocumentFragment(); 2) add each element to it in the loop; 3) insert the container into the page once, after the loop.
Run the audit again to verify the finding is resolved

dom_manipulation_loop.benefit: Long lists appear faster, without slowing down the page.

dynamic_import.title: A module is loaded from a name held in a variable
dynamic_import.risk: __import__() or importlib.import_module() loads the code whose name is held in a variable. If that name comes from a user, they can load any module of your server, including ones that run commands.

steps.action: Locate the vulnerable code pattern in the file
List the allowed modules in a dictionary, MODULES = {"csv": csv, "json": json}, and look the name up there (MODULES.get(name)), refusing any name that is not in it.
Run the audit again to verify the finding is resolved

dynamic_import.benefit: Only the modules you chose can be loaded.

error_suppressor_php.title: Errors from a function call are hidden with the @ operator
error_suppressor_php.risk: The @ placed before a function call hides every error and warning it raises. A missing file, a failed connection or a security problem then goes unnoticed, and the code carries on with a wrong value such as false.

steps.action: Locate the vulnerable code pattern in the file
Remove the @ and handle the failure: 1) test the return value, for example if ($result === false); 2) write the error to the logs or throw an exception.
Run the audit again to verify the finding is resolved

error_suppressor_php.benefit: Failures show up where they happen and can be fixed.

eval_injection_php.title: Text is run as PHP code (eval, assert, create_function)
eval_injection_php.risk: eval(), assert() with a string, create_function() and preg_replace() with the /e option run a piece of text as PHP code. If any part of that text comes from a user, they can run their own code on your server.

steps.action: Locate the vulnerable code pattern in the file

Replace the code built from text with fixed code: read data with json_decode(), pick the action from a list of allowed functions, and write anonymous functions with function () { … } instead of create_function().
Run the audit again to verify the finding is resolved

eval_injection_php.benefit: No text can turn into code on your server.

event_listeners_not_cleaned.title: Event listeners are added but never removed in this file
event_listeners_not_cleaned.risk: This file calls addEventListener() but never removeEventListener(). When a component or element is removed and recreated, the old functions stay attached and keep memory, so the page gets slower and may run the same action several times.

steps.action: Locate the vulnerable code pattern in the file

Remove each listener when it is no longer needed: 1) keep the function in a variable; 2) call removeEventListener() with the same event and function when the element or component is removed (for example in destroy() or the cleanup of useEffect).
Run the audit again to verify the finding is resolved

event_listeners_not_cleaned.benefit: The page no longer keeps old functions in memory or runs them twice.

exposed_test_endpoint.title: A test or debug page is reachable without logging in
exposed_test_endpoint.risk: The application publishes an address such as /test or /debug without asking anyone to log in. These pages often show internal settings or skip security checks, and anyone who finds them can use them.

steps.action: Locate the vulnerable code pattern in the file
Remove this page from the code that goes into production, or protect it with a login check (@login_required) and make it reachable only from your internal network.
Run the audit again to verify the finding is resolved

exposed_test_endpoint.benefit: Visitors can no longer reach your test and debug pages.

express_cors_wildcard.title: Any website can query your server from a visitor's browser
express_cors_wildcard.risk: cors() without options, or with origin: "*", sets CORS (the browser rule that decides which sites may call your server) to accept every site. Any page a visitor opens can then send requests to your server and read its answers.

steps.action: Locate the vulnerable code pattern in the file
List the sites allowed to call your server: app.use(cors({ origin: ["https://app.example.com"] })).
Run the audit again to verify the finding is resolved

express_cors_wildcard.benefit: Only your own sites can use your server from a visitor's browser.

express_no_helmet.title: The Express app sends no security headers (Helmet is missing)
express_no_helmet.risk: This Express app does not use Helmet, a module that adds security headers (instructions the server sends to the browser with each page). Without them, the browser does not block some attacks, such as showing your site inside a hidden frame of another site.

steps.action: Locate the vulnerable code pattern in the file
Add Helmet to the app: 1) install it with npm install helmet; 2) right after const app = express(), add app.use(helmet()).
Run the audit again to verify the finding is resolved

express_no_helmet.benefit: The browser receives the instructions that block the most common attacks on your pages.

extract_usage_php.title: Request data is turned into PHP variables with extract()
extract_usage_php.risk: extract() turns every field of $_GET, $_POST, $_REQUEST or $_SERVER into a variable of the same name. A visitor can add a field such as ?is_admin=1 and overwrite variables your code relies on, for example to skip a check.

steps.action: Locate the vulnerable code pattern in the file
Remove extract() and read each expected field by its name: $name = $_POST['name'] ?? ''.
Run the audit again to verify the finding is resolved

extract_usage_php.benefit: Visitors can no longer change the variables of your code.

file_inclusion_php.title: The PHP file to load is chosen by a variable (include, require)
file_inclusion_php.risk: include and require load and run the PHP file whose name is in the variable. If a user can change that name, they can run another file of the server, read secrets, or even run code from another site.

steps.action: Locate the vulnerable code pattern in the file
Choose the file from a fixed list: check the name with in_array($page, ['home', 'contact'], true), and load only names found in that list.
Run the audit again to verify the finding is resolved

file_inclusion_php.benefit: Only the files you chose can be loaded.

file_too_long.title: File too long (500 lines or more)
file_too_long.risk: This file has 500 lines or more. It probably mixes several subjects, so finding the right place to change takes time, and a change in one part can break another.

steps.action: Locate the vulnerable code pattern in the file
Split the file by subject: move each group of functions or classes that belong together (models, utilities, views…) into its own file, and import them where they are used.
Run the audit again to verify the finding is resolved

file_too_long.benefit: Each file covers one subject and is quicker to read and change.

file_upload_no_validation.title: Uploaded files are accepted without checking their type or size
file_upload_no_validation.risk: This code receives files sent by visitors without checking their name, type or size. An attacker can send a program that the server then runs, a file that replaces another, or a file large enough to fill the disk.

steps.action: Locate the vulnerable code pattern in the file

Check each file before saving it: 1) clean its name with secure_filename(); 2) accept only the expected types, by reading the start of the content and not only the extension; 3) limit the size (MAX_CONTENT_LENGTH); 4) store it outside the folders the site serves.
Run the audit again to verify the finding is resolved

file_upload_no_validation.benefit: Only the files you expect reach your server, and none of them can be run.

flask_debug_enabled.title: Flask in debug mode: visitors can run code on the server
flask_debug_enabled.risk: app.run(debug=True) turns on the Werkzeug debugger, which opens a console in the browser when an error occurs. Anyone who reaches it can run commands on the server.

steps.action: Locate the vulnerable code pattern in the file
Turn debug mode off in production: read it from an environment variable (debug=os.environ.get("FLASK_DEBUG") == "True") so that it is only on for local development.
Run the audit again to verify the finding is resolved

flask_debug_enabled.benefit: Visitors can no longer run commands on your server through the debugger.

flask_secret_key_weak.title: The secret key of Flask is written in the code
flask_secret_key_weak.risk: Flask signs the session cookies with secret_key. Anyone who reads this key in the code can forge a session, for example to log in as an administrator.

steps.action: Locate the vulnerable code pattern in the file

Remove the key from the code: 1) read it from an environment variable (app.secret_key = os.environ["FLASK_SECRET_KEY"]); 2) generate a new one with os.urandom(32).hex(), since the old one stays in the history.
Run the audit again to verify the finding is resolved

flask_secret_key_weak.benefit: Reading your code no longer lets anyone forge a session.

focus_outline_removed.title: The outline that shows keyboard focus is removed
focus_outline_removed.risk: The code sets outline to none or 0: the browser no longer draws the outline around the focused element (the one that receives the keyboard keys). People who use the keyboard instead of a mouse no longer see where they are on the page.

steps.action: Locate the vulnerable code pattern in the file
Keep a visible focus outline: remove the code that sets outline to none or 0, or replace it with a visible style on :focus-visible, such as outline: 2px solid #4A90D9.
Run the audit again to verify the finding is resolved

focus_outline_removed.benefit: Keyboard users always see where they are on the page.

format_string_vuln.title: Text built with format() includes data from the request
format_string_vuln.risk: The code puts request data into a text with .format(). Shown as is in a page, that text can carry a script; and if the template itself comes from the user, fields like {0.__class__} reveal internal data.

steps.action: Locate the vulnerable code pattern in the file

Treat the value as data: 1) keep the template a fixed text written in your code, never one from the request; 2) escape the value for where it goes, html.escape(name) for a page, logger.info("User action: %s", action) for a log.
Run the audit again to verify the finding is resolved

format_string_vuln.benefit: Request data stays plain data and never changes the text around it.

gha_excessive_permissions.title: The automation gets every write right on the project
gha_excessive_permissions.risk: permissions: write-all gives the automation's GitHub access key the right to change everything: code, releases, issues and settings. A faulty or booby-trapped tool run by the automation can use those rights against your project.

steps.action: Locate the vulnerable code pattern in the file
Replace permissions: write-all with read-only access (contents: read), then grant each write right only to the task that needs it.
Run the audit again to verify the finding is resolved

gha_excessive_permissions.benefit: A faulty tool in your automation can do far less damage to your project.

gha_expression_injection.title: Text that anyone can write is inserted straight into a command
gha_expression_injection.risk: The file inserts the title or text of an issue, change request or comment straight into the automation with ${{ … }}. Anyone can write that text, and a crafted title becomes a command that runs with your secrets.

steps.action: Locate the vulnerable code pattern in the file
Pass the text through a variable: 1) under the step, add env: TITLE: ${{ github.event.issue.title }}; 2) in run:, write "$TITLE" in double quotes instead of ${{ … }}.
Run the audit again to verify the finding is resolved

gha_expression_injection.benefit: A title or comment stays plain text and can never run as a command.

gha_missing_permissions.title: The automation file does not limit the rights of its GitHub access key
gha_missing_permissions.risk: This automation file (the file that tests and publishes the project with GitHub Actions) has no permissions: section. Its GitHub access key then gets the repository's default rights, often the right to change everything. A faulty or booby-trapped tool run by the automation could alter your code or your releases.

steps.action: Locate the vulnerable code pattern in the file

Limit the rights of the access key: 1) at the top of the file, before jobs:, add a permissions: section with the line contents: read; 2) add a write right only where a task needs it, for example pull-requests: write.
Run the audit again to verify the finding is resolved

gha_missing_permissions.benefit: A faulty or booby-trapped tool in your automation can read your code but not change it.

gha_unguarded_comment_trigger.title: Any comment, from anyone, starts the automation
gha_unguarded_comment_trigger.risk: The automation starts on issue_comment, that is on every comment on an issue or change request, with no condition on its text. Anyone who can comment can start it, and with it your secrets and write rights.

steps.action: Locate the vulnerable code pattern in the file
Start the task only when the comment begins with a precise command and comes from a commenter with a trusted role (owner, member or collaborator).
Run the audit again to verify the finding is resolved

gha_unguarded_comment_trigger.benefit: Only the commands you chose, from people you trust, start the automation.

gitlab_unsafe_variables.title: Text chosen by any contributor is placed in a GitLab CI command
gitlab_unsafe_variables.risk: Your .gitlab-ci.yml file uses the branch name, the merge request title or the commit message (the text that describes a change). Anyone who proposes a change chooses these texts, and without quotes such a text can change the arguments of the command. Given to eval or sh -c, it runs as commands on the build machine, which holds your secrets.

steps.action: Locate the vulnerable code pattern in the file

Treat these variables as untrusted text: 1) put them in double quotes, as in "$CI_COMMIT_REF_NAME"; 2) remove special characters before using them, as in the example; 3) never pass them to eval or sh -c.
Run the audit again to verify the finding is resolved

gitlab_unsafe_variables.benefit: A branch name or a message can no longer run commands on your build machine.

graphql_introspection_enabled.title: GraphQL lets anyone list the whole API
graphql_introspection_enabled.risk: Introspection (a GraphQL feature that describes every type and field) is turned on explicitly. In production, anyone can download the full map of your API, hidden and internal fields included, and pick what to attack.

steps.action: Locate the vulnerable code pattern in the file
Turn introspection off in production, for example with Ariadne: GraphQL(schema, introspection=os.environ.get("ENV") != "production").
Run the audit again to verify the finding is resolved

graphql_introspection_enabled.benefit: Visitors no longer get a map of your API.

graphql_no_depth_limit.title: GraphQL accepts queries nested without limit
graphql_no_depth_limit.risk: This file sets up GraphQL with no limit on how deeply a query can nest fields. One small query that loops between linked objects can make the server compute millions of results and stop answering.

steps.action: Locate the vulnerable code pattern in the file

Limit the depth of accepted queries to about 10 levels: add depth_limit_validator(max_depth=10) from graphene.validation to the validation rules, or the QueryDepthLimiter(max_depth=10) extension with Strawberry.
Run the audit again to verify the finding is resolved

graphql_no_depth_limit.benefit: A single query can no longer use up the server's resources.

hardcoded_internal_ip.title: An internal network address is written in the code
hardcoded_internal_ip.risk: This private IP address (10.x, 192.168.x, 172.16 to 172.31) shows anyone who reads the code how your internal network is organized. It also ties the code to one environment: it breaks when the server moves.

steps.action: Locate the vulnerable code pattern in the file
Read the address from an environment variable or a configuration file: DB_HOST = os.environ.get("DB_HOST", "localhost").
Run the audit again to verify the finding is resolved

hardcoded_internal_ip.benefit: The code no longer reveals your network and runs in any environment.

hardcoded_secret.title: A password or secret key is written in the code
hardcoded_secret.risk: A password, an access key or a token (a secret code that opens a service) is written in clear in this file. Anyone who can read the code or its history, now or later, can use it to access your services.

steps.action: Locate the vulnerable code pattern in the file

Remove the secret from the code: 1) read it from an environment variable (os.environ["API_KEY"]) or from your secret manager; 2) replace it with a new value at the service that issued it, since the old one stays in the history.
Run the audit again to verify the finding is resolved

hardcoded_secret.benefit: Reading your code no longer gives access to your services.

hardcoded_ui_string.title: Text shown to users is written directly in the code
hardcoded_ui_string.risk: A placeholder or title attribute (the hint shown in an empty field or on hover) holds text written in the page, not in a translation file. It always appears in the same language, and every change of wording means editing the page.

steps.action: Locate the vulnerable code pattern in the file

Move the text into your translation files: 1) give it a key, such as form.email, with one translation per language; 2) link the attribute to that key, such as data-i18n="[placeholder]form.email" with i18next.
Run the audit again to verify the finding is resolved

hardcoded_ui_string.benefit: The interface can be translated without touching the code.

homebrew_auth.title: A password is checked with == instead of a password function
homebrew_auth.risk: Comparing the password with == means it is stored as it is, readable by anyone who gets the database. The comparison also stops at the first wrong character, and the time it takes can help an attacker guess it.

steps.action: Locate the vulnerable code pattern in the file
Store a password hash (a one-way fingerprint) made with bcrypt or Argon2id, and check it with bcrypt.checkpw(password.encode(), stored_hash).
Run the audit again to verify the finding is resolved

homebrew_auth.benefit: Passwords stay unreadable, even for someone who gets the database.

http_no_tls.title: An address uses http:// instead of https://
http_no_tls.risk: The code connects to an address that starts with http://, so the data travels unencrypted. Anyone on the same network, such as a public Wi-Fi or a compromised router, can read or change it on the way.

steps.action: Locate the vulnerable code pattern in the file
Replace http:// with https:// in this address, after checking that the server at that address accepts https.
Run the audit again to verify the finding is resolved

http_no_tls.benefit: Data exchanged with this address can no longer be read or changed on the way.

img_no_alt.title: An image has no text alternative (alt)
img_no_alt.risk: This has no alt attribute. Blind people using a screen reader (software that reads the page aloud) hear the file name or nothing, and miss what the image shows. The text is also missing when the image fails to load.

steps.action: Locate the vulnerable code pattern in the file
Add an alt attribute that says what the image shows, for example alt="Team photo", or alt="" if the image is only decorative.
Run the audit again to verify the finding is resolved

img_no_alt.benefit: Everyone, including blind visitors, gets the information the image carries.

inline_style_js.title: A style is set directly in JavaScript instead of a CSS class
inline_style_js.risk: The code gives an element a fixed look with element.style, such as a color or a size written as text. These values are scattered in the code, override your style sheets, and make the look of the site hard to keep consistent.

steps.action: Locate the vulnerable code pattern in the file
Move the look to your style sheet: 1) define it in a CSS class; 2) add or remove that class with element.classList.add() and element.classList.remove().
Run the audit again to verify the finding is resolved

inline_style_js.benefit: The look of the site is defined in one place and stays consistent.

input_no_label.title: A form field has no label
input_no_label.risk: This <input> field has no aria-label and no id, so no <label> can name it. Blind people using a screen reader (software that reads the page aloud) hear only a generic word, without knowing what to type.

steps.action: Locate the vulnerable code pattern in the file
Give the field a name: 1) add id="email" to the <input>; 2) add <label for="email">Email</label> next to it. Without room for visible text, add aria-label="Email" to the field.
Run the audit again to verify the finding is resolved

input_no_label.benefit: Screen reader users know what to type in each field.

insecure_cloud_config.title: A cloud resource is open to the whole internet
insecure_cloud_config.risk: The code makes a cloud resource public: S3 bucket readable by all, firewall open to every address (0.0.0.0/0), or database reachable from the internet. Anyone can then read the files or try to get into the database.

steps.action: Locate the vulnerable code pattern in the file
Keep resources private by default: ACL='private' with BlockPublicAccess turned on, firewall rules limited to known addresses, and PubliclyAccessible=False for databases.
Run the audit again to verify the finding is resolved

insecure_cloud_config.benefit: Your cloud files and databases are only reachable by those you choose.

insecure_cookie.title: A cookie is set without HttpOnly or Secure
insecure_cookie.risk: The cookie is created with none of its protections. Without HttpOnly, a script injected into the page can read it and steal the session. Without Secure, it also travels unencrypted over HTTP, readable by anyone on the network.

steps.action: Locate the vulnerable code pattern in the file
Add the protections to the call: response.set_cookie("session_id", token, httponly=True, secure=True, samesite="Lax").
Run the audit again to verify the finding is resolved

insecure_cookie.benefit: Scripts cannot read the cookie, and it only travels encrypted.

insecure_local_storage.title: A token or a password is saved in localStorage
insecure_local_storage.risk: localStorage.setItem() saves a token (a secret code that opens a session), a password or a key in the browser, where any script of the page can read it. If an attacker injects a script, even through a library, they get the value and can use the account.

steps.action: Locate the vulnerable code pattern in the file

Keep secrets out of localStorage: 1) have the server send the login token in a cookie marked HttpOnly and Secure, which scripts cannot read; 2) keep other short-lived secrets in a variable, in memory only.
Run the audit again to verify the finding is resolved

insecure_local_storage.benefit: A script injected into the page can no longer read your users' tokens.

insecure_random.title: Insecure RNG
insecure_random.risk: Math.random() is predictable and must not be used for tokens, OTPs or keys.

steps.action: Locate the vulnerable code pattern in the file
Use crypto.getRandomValues() or crypto.randomUUID() for sensitive values.
Run the audit again to verify the finding is resolved

insecure_random.benefit: Unpredictable tokens and keys, resistant to attacks (CWE-330).

insufficient_key_size.title: An encryption key of 1024 bits or less is created
insufficient_key_size.risk: The code asks for a key of 512, 768 or 1024 bits, for RSA for example. Keys this short can be broken with today's computing power, so anyone who records your encrypted data or signatures can read or forge them.

steps.action: Locate the vulnerable code pattern in the file
Generate keys of at least 2048 bits, ideally 3072 or more: RSA.generate(3072), or key_size=3072 with rsa.generate_private_key().
Run the audit again to verify the finding is resolved

insufficient_key_size.benefit: Your encrypted data and signatures stay safe for years.

jndi_injection_java.title: A JNDI lookup uses a name that may come from outside (Log4Shell)
jndi_injection_java.risk: The code calls lookup() with a name that is not a fixed text, in a file that uses JNDI. JNDI (the Java service that finds resources by name) can then load and run code from an attacker's server, as in the Log4Shell attack.

steps.action: Locate the vulnerable code pattern in the file
Close the hole: 1) pass only fixed names to lookup(), such as ctx.lookup("java:comp/env/jdbc/mydb"), never a value from a request; 2) update Log4j to version 2.17.1 or later.
Run the audit again to verify the finding is resolved

jndi_injection_java.benefit: Names sent by an attacker can no longer load code onto your server.

jwt_hardcoded_secret.title: The key that signs login tokens (JWT) is written in the code
jwt_hardcoded_secret.risk: Login tokens (JWT) prove who the user is because only the server knows the key that signs them. Here the key is in the code, so anyone who reads it can make a token for any user, administrators included.

steps.action: Locate the vulnerable code pattern in the file
Remove the key from the code: 1) read it from an environment variable (os.environ["JWT_SECRET"]) or from your secret manager; 2) replace it with a new key, since the old one stays in the history.
Run the audit again to verify the finding is resolved

jwt_hardcoded_secret.benefit: Reading your code no longer lets anyone make login tokens.

jwt_none_algorithm.title: Login tokens (JWT) are accepted without checking their signature
jwt_none_algorithm.risk: A JWT is a token (a signed code that proves who the user is). Here the code accepts the "none" algorithm or turns off the check (verify=False), so anyone can write a token saying they are an administrator.

steps.action: Locate the vulnerable code pattern in the file
Always check the signature and name the accepted algorithm: jwt.decode(token, SECRET_KEY, algorithms=["HS256"]), never "none" and never verify=False.
Run the audit again to verify the finding is resolved

jwt_none_algorithm.benefit: Only tokens signed by your server are accepted.

ldap_injection_csharp.title: An LDAP search filter is built by joining text with +
ldap_injection_csharp.risk: The filter of an LDAP search (a query to the company directory, such as Active Directory) is built by joining text with +. A user who types characters like * or ) can change the search, for example to log in without a valid password or to list every account.

steps.action: Locate the vulnerable code pattern in the file
Escape the user value before it goes into the filter: replace \ * ( ) and the null character with \5c, \2a, \28, \29 and \00, or accept only letters and digits in it.
Run the audit again to verify the finding is resolved

ldap_injection_csharp.benefit: A user value can no longer change the meaning of your directory searches.

ldap_injection_java.title: LDAP injection (Java)
ldap_injection_java.risk: String concatenation in LDAP search filters allows query manipulation and authentication bypass (CWE-90, OWASP A03).

steps.action: Locate the vulnerable code pattern in the file
Use parameterized searches with SearchControls or escape input with LdapEncoder.filterEncode().
Run the audit again to verify the finding is resolved

ldap_injection_java.benefit: LDAP queries safe from injection attacks.

ldap_injection_python.title: LDAP injection (Python)
ldap_injection_python.risk: String concatenation in LDAP filters allows attackers to modify queries and bypass authentication (CWE-90, OWASP A03).

steps.action: Locate the vulnerable code pattern in the file
Use parameterized LDAP filters with ldap.filter.filter_format() or escape user input with ldap.filter.escape_filter_chars().
Run the audit again to verify the finding is resolved

ldap_injection_python.benefit: LDAP queries safe from injection attacks.

local_time_usage.title: A date is taken in the server's local time, without a time zone
local_time_usage.risk: datetime.now() gives the time of the place where the server runs, with no time zone attached. Two servers in different places, or a change to summer time, give different or ambiguous times, which mixes up the order of events.

steps.action: Locate the vulnerable code pattern in the file
Take the time in universal time with its zone: write datetime.now(timezone.utc) (from datetime import timezone), and convert it to local time only to display it.
Run the audit again to verify the finding is resolved

local_time_usage.benefit: All your dates are comparable, whatever the server and the season.

log_injection.title: A value written to the log can add fake lines to it
log_injection.risk: This log message includes a value that may come from a user, without removing its line breaks. An attacker can then add fake lines to the log, for example to hide an attack or blame someone else.

steps.action: Locate the vulnerable code pattern in the file
Remove the line breaks from the value before writing it: value.replace("\r", "").replace("\n", ""), then pass it as a parameter (logger.info("Login: %s", value)).
Run the audit again to verify the finding is resolved

log_injection.benefit: Each line of the log matches a real event.

manual_createelement.title: Page elements are built by hand with document.createElement
manual_createelement.risk: Several document.createElement calls in a row build a part of the page in code, one piece at a time. Larger parts built this way are long, hard to read, and easy to break when the page changes.

steps.action: Locate the vulnerable code pattern in the file
Describe larger parts of the page as HTML, in a <template> element or a component of your interface library (React, Vue), and keep createElement for single elements.
Run the audit again to verify the finding is resolved

manual_createelement.benefit: The structure of the page can be read at a glance and changed safely.

mass_assignment_laravel.title: A record is created or updated with every field of the request
mass_assignment_laravel.risk: The code passes $request->all() to create() or update(), so every field of the form goes into the database. A visitor can add a field such as is_admin=1 or balance=9999 and change data they should never touch.

steps.action: Locate the vulnerable code pattern in the file
Pass only the fields you expect: $request->only(['name', 'email']) or $request->validated(), and list the fields allowed in $fillable on the model.
Run the audit again to verify the finding is resolved

mass_assignment_laravel.benefit: Visitors can only change the fields you chose.

missing_auth_decorator.title: A sensitive page (admin, changes to data) does not require logging in
missing_auth_decorator.risk: This route, such as /admin or /api/delete, has no login check (@login_required or similar). Anyone who knows its address can use it without an account.

steps.action: Locate the vulnerable code pattern in the file
Add a login check to the route (@login_required, @jwt_required or your own), and a role check if only some users may use it.
Run the audit again to verify the finding is resolved

missing_auth_decorator.benefit: Only logged-in users can reach your sensitive pages.

missing_change_management.title: The code force-pushes to Git or changes tables directly
missing_change_management.risk: The code overwrites the Git history with push --force, or changes the structure of tables with ALTER or DROP TABLE. These changes skip review and leave no record to undo them, so a mistake reaches production unseen.

steps.action: Locate the vulnerable code pattern in the file

Send each change through review: 1) change tables with versioned migrations (Alembic, Django migrations); 2) push to a branch, without --force, and merge it after review into a protected branch (one that only accepts reviewed changes).
Run the audit again to verify the finding is resolved

missing_change_management.benefit: Each change is reviewed and can be undone.

missing_csp_header.title: Browsers are not told which scripts your pages may load
missing_csp_header.risk: Your web application does not send a Content-Security-Policy header (a list of the sources your pages may load scripts and content from). If an attacker manages to insert a script into a page, the browser runs it without restriction.

steps.action: Locate the vulnerable code pattern in the file

Send this header from your application, starting with a strict policy: with Flask, install flask-talisman and add Talisman(app, content_security_policy={"default-src": "'self'"}); with Django, install django-csp.
Run the audit again to verify the finding is resolved

missing_csp_header.benefit: A script inserted by an attacker is blocked by the browser.

missing_data_retention.title: Personal data is kept with no way to delete it
missing_data_retention.risk: This file stores personal data (email, phone, address, date of birth…) but has no code to delete or anonymize it. You keep it forever, which breaks the GDPR rule of keeping data only as long as needed, and any leak exposes all of it.

steps.action: Locate the vulnerable code pattern in the file

Decide how long you keep this data, then: 1) add a method that deletes or anonymizes a record (for example anonymize(), which replaces the email with deleted_<id>@anonymized.local); 2) run it regularly on the records older than that period.
Run the audit again to verify the finding is resolved

missing_data_retention.benefit: You keep personal data only as long as needed, as the GDPR requires.

missing_frame_protection.title: Missing X-Frame-Options
missing_frame_protection.risk: Without X-Frame-Options or CSP frame-ancestors, the page can be embedded in iframes enabling clickjacking attacks (CWE-1021).

steps.action: Locate the vulnerable code pattern in the file
Add X-Frame-Options: DENY or SAMEORIGIN header, or use CSP frame-ancestors directive.
Run the audit again to verify the finding is resolved

missing_frame_protection.benefit: Prevents clickjacking attacks by blocking unauthorized framing of the page.

missing_health_check.title: The application has no address to check that it works
missing_health_check.risk: Your application has web pages but no health address (such as /health) that answers "I am working". The tools that spread traffic or restart the service cannot tell when it is down, so visitors keep landing on a broken server.

steps.action: Locate the vulnerable code pattern in the file

Add a route that answers when the application works, for example @app.route("/health") returning {"status": "ok"}, and give its address to your hosting (load balancer, container platform) as the health check.
Run the audit again to verify the finding is resolved

missing_health_check.benefit: A failure is noticed at once, and traffic goes to the servers that work.

missing_hsts.title: Browsers are not told to always use https:// for your site
missing_hsts.risk: Your web application does not send the Strict-Transport-Security header (an instruction telling browsers to always use https:// for your site). On a visitor's first connection, an attacker on the same network can force an unencrypted connection and steal session cookies.

steps.action: Locate the vulnerable code pattern in the file
Send this header from your application: with Flask, install flask-talisman and add Talisman(app); with Django, set SECURE_HSTS_SECONDS = 31536000 (one year) in settings.py.
Run the audit again to verify the finding is resolved

missing_hsts.benefit: Browsers always connect to your site with encryption.

missing_mfa_csharp.title: Login relies on the password alone, without a second check
missing_mfa_csharp.risk: Users log in with a password only, without a second factor (for example a code from a phone app). A password that is stolen, guessed or reused from another site is then enough to take over the account.

steps.action: Locate the vulnerable code pattern in the file
Add a second step after the password: a one-time code from a phone app (TOTP), checked with TwoFactorAuthenticatorSignInAsync() of ASP.NET Core Identity, at least for administrators.
Run the audit again to verify the finding is resolved

missing_mfa_csharp.benefit: A stolen password is no longer enough to take over an account.

missing_mfa_java.title: Login relies on a password only, with no second check
missing_mfa_java.risk: This file logs users in with Spring Security (AuthenticationManager, authenticate()) and contains no trace of a second factor, such as a one-time code. A stolen or guessed password is then enough to take over an account.

steps.action: Locate the vulnerable code pattern in the file

Add a second step to the login: 1) after the password check, ask for a one-time code from an authenticator app, using a library such as dev.samstevens.totp; 2) open the session only when that code is correct.
Run the audit again to verify the finding is resolved

missing_mfa_java.benefit: A stolen password alone no longer opens an account.

missing_mfa_javascript.title: Login relies on a password alone, without a second factor
missing_mfa_javascript.risk: The file logs users in with a password (passport.authenticate, signInWithPassword) and checks no second factor (a code from a phone app). Whoever steals or guesses a password enters the account.

steps.action: Locate the vulnerable code pattern in the file
Add a second step after the password: check a one-time code with otplib or speakeasy.totp.verify(), at least for administrator accounts.
Run the audit again to verify the finding is resolved

missing_mfa_javascript.benefit: A stolen password is no longer enough to enter an account.

missing_mfa_php.title: Login relies on the password alone, with no second step
missing_mfa_php.risk: This file logs users in with Auth::attempt() or Auth::login() and asks for no one-time code, such as a code from a phone app. A stolen or guessed password is then enough to take over the account.

steps.action: Locate the vulnerable code pattern in the file
Add a second login step: after the password, ask for a one-time code and check it with a library such as pragmarx/google2fa-laravel (Google2FA::verifyKey()), at least for administrator accounts.
Run the audit again to verify the finding is resolved

missing_mfa_php.benefit: A stolen password is no longer enough to enter an account.

missing_mfa_python.title: Login relies on the password alone, without a second check
missing_mfa_python.risk: Users log in with a password only, without a second factor (for example a code from a phone app). A password that is stolen, guessed or reused from another site is then enough to take over the account.

steps.action: Locate the vulnerable code pattern in the file
Add a second step after the password: a one-time code from a phone app (TOTP, with pyotp or django-otp), at least for administrators.
Run the audit again to verify the finding is resolved

missing_mfa_python.benefit: A stolen password is no longer enough to take over an account.

missing_monitoring.title: Sensitive operations leave no trace in the logs
missing_monitoring.risk: This file handles web requests (logins, payments, deletions…) but writes nothing to the logs. If someone abuses it, you will not notice, and you will have no record to understand what happened.

steps.action: Locate the vulnerable code pattern in the file

Log the important operations of this file: 1) add import logging and logger = logging.getLogger(__name__) at the top; 2) call logger.info(...) for each login, data change or payment, and logger.warning(...) for each refused attempt.
Run the audit again to verify the finding is resolved

missing_monitoring.benefit: You see abuse when it happens and can understand an incident afterwards.

missing_referrer_policy.title: Missing Referrer-Policy
missing_referrer_policy.risk: Without Referrer-Policy header, sensitive data in URLs (tokens, session IDs) may leak to third-party sites via the Referer header (CWE-200).

steps.action: Locate the vulnerable code pattern in the file
Add Referrer-Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin or no-referrer header. Configure at web server or framework level.
Run the audit again to verify the finding is resolved

missing_referrer_policy.benefit: Prevents leakage of sensitive URL data to external sites.

missing_security_docs.title: A security function has no description
missing_security_docs.risk: This function handles security (encryption, passwords, access, checks) but has no description (docstring: the text in triple quotes under its first line). Reviewers cannot check that it does what it should, and a later change can weaken it unnoticed.

steps.action: Locate the vulnerable code pattern in the file

Write, right under the line def name(...):, a text between triple quotes that says what the function protects, how (which algorithm or check), what it receives and returns, and what it assumes about its input.
Run the audit again to verify the finding is resolved

sql_injection_whereraw_php.risk: The SQL given to whereRaw(), havingRaw(), selectRaw() or orderByRaw() is built by joining text with the . operator, outside the protection of Laravel. If one piece comes from a user, that user can add their own SQL, for example to read or delete all data.

steps.action: Locate the vulnerable code pattern in the file
Put a ? in the SQL and pass the values in a separate list: whereRaw('name = ?', [$name]), or use the normal Laravel methods such as where('name', $name).
Run the audit again to verify the finding is resolved

sql_injection_whereraw_php.benefit: A value from a user can no longer change your queries.

sql_injection_wpdb.title: A WordPress query run by $wpdb is built by pasting text together
sql_injection_wpdb.risk: The SQL given to $wpdb->query(), get_results(), get_row(), get_var() or get_col() is built by joining text with . or +. If one piece comes from a user, that user can add their own SQL, for example to read or delete all data.

Run the audit again to verify the finding is resolved

sql_injection_wpdb.benefit: A value from a user can no longer change your queries.

ssl_bypass_csharp.title: A callback accepts every server certificate without checking it
ssl_bypass_csharp.risk: Here the check of the server certificate (its proof of identity) is replaced by a callback that always returns true, or by DangerousAcceptAnyServerCertificateValidator. The program then accepts any server, so someone on the network can pose as it and read or change the data, passwords included.

steps.action: Locate the vulnerable code pattern in the file

Run the audit again to verify the finding is resolved

ssl_bypass_csharp.benefit: Your program only talks to the real server, and the exchanged data stays private.

ssl_bypass_java.title: Certificate or host name checks are turned off for HTTPS
ssl_bypass_java.risk: The code trusts every certificate (a TrustAllCerts class) or replaces the host name check with its own code, often to accept any name. Someone on the network, for example on public Wi-Fi, can then pose as the server and read or change the data, passwords included.

steps.action: Locate the vulnerable code pattern in the file
Let Java check connections again: 1) remove the custom TrustManager and HostnameVerifier; 2) for a test server, add its certificate to a trust store (a file of trusted certificates).
Run the audit again to verify the finding is resolved

ssl_bypass_java.benefit: Nobody on the network can pose as the servers your application connects to.

ssrf_java.benefit: Prevention of SSRF attacks in Java applications.

ssrf_javascript.risk: fetch()/axios with user-controlled URLs allow SSRF attacks (OWASP A10, CWE-918).

steps.action: Locate the vulnerable code pattern in the file

Run the audit again to verify the finding is resolved

ssrf_javascript.benefit: Prevention of SSRF attacks in Node.js applications.

ssrf_php.title: Server-Side Request Forgery (PHP)
ssrf_php.risk: file_get_contents()/curl with user-controlled URLs allow SSRF attacks (OWASP A10, CWE-918).

Run the audit again to verify the finding is resolved

ssrf_php.benefit: Prevention of SSRF attacks in PHP applications.

ssrf_python.title: The server fetches an address the user can choose
ssrf_python.risk: Your server sends a web request to an address held in a variable, which may come from the user. An attacker can then make your server call internal services that are not reachable from outside, or read cloud access keys.

steps.action: Locate the vulnerable code pattern in the file

Only allow the addresses you expect: 1) keep a list of the permitted domains and refuse any other one; 2) refuse the addresses that point to your own network (127.x, 10.x, 172.16.x to 172.31.x, 192.168.x, 169.254.x).
Run the audit again to verify the finding is resolved

ssrf_python.benefit: Your server only calls the addresses you chose.

ssti_javascript.title: A template is compiled from a text string with EJS, Pug or Nunjucks
ssti_javascript.risk: ejs.render(), pug.render() and similar calls turn a text into a page template (a model of the page with code inside). If that text comes from a user, the user can put code in it and run it on the server.

steps.action: Locate the vulnerable code pattern in the file
Keep templates in files and pass the user's text as data only: ejs.renderFile("views/page.ejs", { content: req.body.content }) or pug.renderFile("views/page.pug", { content }).
Run the audit again to verify the finding is resolved

ssti_javascript.benefit: Users can fill in your pages but cannot change the code they run.

ssti_python.title: Server-Side Template Injection (Python)
ssti_python.risk: User input passed directly to template rendering (Jinja2, Mako, Django) allows arbitrary code execution on the server (CWE-1336).

steps.action: Locate the vulnerable code pattern in the file
Never render user input as a template string. Use template files with context variables. Enable Jinja2 sandboxed environment.
Run the audit again to verify the finding is resolved

ssti_python.benefit: Prevents remote code execution via template engine exploitation.

svg_inline_html.title: An SVG drawing is written directly in the HTML page
svg_inline_html.risk: The <svg> drawing (an icon or image described as code) is written inside the page. Repeated on many pages, it makes them heavier, and each copy must be changed by hand.

steps.action: Locate the vulnerable code pattern in the file
Save the drawing in its own .svg file and show it with , unless a script must change its colors or shape.
Run the audit again to verify the finding is resolved

svg_inline_html.benefit: Pages are lighter and each drawing is changed in one place.

svg_scriptable_content.title: An SVG image contains code that runs
svg_scriptable_content.risk: This SVG file contains a <script> tag, an attribute such as onload or a foreignObject element. The browser runs this code when it shows the image.

steps.action: Locate the vulnerable code pattern in the file

Clean the SVG file: 1) remove the <script> tags, the on… attributes and the foreignObject elements; 2) pass SVG files sent by visitors through a cleaning library such as DOMPurify before showing them.
Run the audit again to verify the finding is resolved

svg_scriptable_content.benefit: Your images can no longer run code.

system_out_java.title: Messages are written with System.out or System.err
system_out_java.risk: These messages go straight to the console, with no level, no date and no control over where they end up. In production they are lost or mixed together, and debug output can reveal data that should stay private.

steps.action: Locate the vulnerable code pattern in the file
Replace each call with a logger (the tool that writes the program's log) such as SLF4J, at the right level: logger.debug("Processing: {}", data) for details, logger.error(...) for errors.
Run the audit again to verify the finding is resolved

system_out_java.benefit: Messages are dated, sorted by importance and kept where you can find them.
